newsitem.title: UK: Rebel entry to Zaire mining city buoys cobalt price.
newsitem.headline: Rebel entry to Zaire mining city buoys cobalt price.

text.p: The world price of cobalt was buoyed on Wednesday by concerns about supply from Zaire, a major producer, as rebel forces entered its second city, Lubumbashi.

Traders said, however, that the fall of Lubumbashi, at the heart of the mineral-rich Shaba province, had been expected and already factored in both to short-term metals prices and longer views about Zaire supply.
High grade cobalt was bid at $24 per pound, compared with $19 earlier this year but unchanged from Tuesday.
Industry officials believe that output may be briefly disrupted but that fighting will soon end and that any new government may invest more money in the ailing minerals industry.
The state metals producer, Gecamines, closed its headquarters in Lubumbashi on Monday as rebels advanced.
The market for cobalt firmed on that news but showed little reaction to news of the rebel entry to the city on Wednesday, said a trader.
"The situation in Zaire is worrying a lot of people but the country has not burned down," he added.
Traders do not think that anyone who secures effective control of Shaba region would want to curtail production of a hard currency earner like cobalt.

Zaire has recently been producing around 5,000 tonnes of cobalt and 40,000 tonnes of copper a year. The copper is marginal to world supply but the cobalt forms roughly one fifth of global supply of all grades of that metal.
Analysts say stocks of up to 600 tonnes are adequate for the time being. Cobalt is used in the aerospace and battery industries.
